keyword: what to write in a journal
title: What to Write in a Journal: 50 Ideas and Examples
description: Not sure what to write in a journal? Get 50 easy ideas, a simple entry formula, real journal examples, and a page to start writing right now.
h1: What to write in a journal: ideas, examples and a simple formula
card: Never stare at a blank page
intro: You can write anything in a journal: what happened today, how you feel, what you are grateful for, what worries you, what you want, and what you learned. If you are stuck, use a simple formula: **one thing that happened, one feeling, one thought about it.** Three sentences is a real journal entry.

writer.title: Today I want to write about...
writer.hint: One thing that happened, one feeling, one thought about it.

sections.h2: The easy formula for any journal entry

blocks.p: Most people freeze because they think a journal entry has to be deep or well written. It does not. Nobody grades it. A good entry is simply an honest one.
When you do not know what to write in a journal entry, answer these three questions in order:

ol: **What happened?** One moment from today, big or small.
**How did I feel?** Name the feeling in one or two words.
**What do I think about it?** Why it mattered, what you learned, or what you want to do next.

example.label: Journal entry
example.text:
My boss asked me to lead Friday's meeting.
I felt proud, then nervous about an hour later.
I think I am scared of being watched, not of the work.
Tonight I will write down the three points I want to make.

blocks.tip: If even three sentences feels like too much, write one line. A [one line a day journal](/one-line-a-day-journal/) is still a journal.

sections.h2: What to write in a journal every day

blocks.p: If you want to write daily, it helps to have a few go-to topics so you never start from nothing. Rotate through these:

ul: **Your day in three lines.** Morning, afternoon, evening.
**Three good things.** Small is fine: a hot shower, a kind text, a song.
**Your mood and why.** Rate it from 1 to 10, then explain the number.
**One thing you learned.** A fact, a skill, or something about a person.
**Tomorrow's one goal.** The single thing that would make tomorrow feel good.
**A conversation you keep thinking about.** What was said and what you wish you had said.
**What your body needs.** Sleep, water, a walk, a break.
**A question for yourself.** Write it down, even if you cannot answer it yet.

blocks.p: For a fresh question each day, try our [daily journal prompts](/daily-journal-prompts/) or use a [daily journal](/daily-journal/) page with the questions already set out.

blocks.p: Need even more? Browse 100+ [journal prompts](/journal-prompts/) or our list of [journal ideas](/journal-ideas/).

sections.h2: What to write in a journal: examples

blocks.p: Here are three short entries using ideas from the list above. Notice that none of them are long or fancy.

example.label: Gratitude entry
example.title: Three good things
example.text:
1. Pancakes with my sister, the burnt ones too.
2. The sun came out for our walk.
3. Mom called just to say hi.
I almost said today was boring. It was not.

example.label: Feelings entry
example.text:
I have been avoiding the dentist for months.
I think I am scared it will hurt and cost a lot.
Most likely: a cleaning and one small filling.
I will call tomorrow at 9 before I talk myself out of it.

example.label: Goal entry
example.title: One year from now
example.text:
I want to be able to run 5 km without stopping.
Right now I can run for about four minutes.
First step: three short runs this week.
I will write how each one felt.

blocks.p: See many more in our [journal examples](/journal-examples/), including dream, travel, prayer and venting entries.

sections.h2: What to write based on why you journal

blocks.p: The best things to write depend on what you want from your journal. Find your reason below and start there.

head: If you want to
Write about
Try this line
rows: Events, people, places, food, small details
"Today, the thing I want to remember is..."
Worries, what you can control, one next step
"The thing on my mind is... and I can..."
Good moments, people you love, small wins
Ideas, overheard lines, things you noticed
"Something I saw today that I want to use..."

blocks.h3: Write the hard days and the good days

blocks.p: It is tempting to only write when something goes wrong, or only when life looks nice. Try to record both. Years later, the entries about hard times often mean the most, because they show you how you got through. The good entries remind you that bad stretches end.

Instead of retelling your whole day, pick one moment that stirred a feeling and describe it closely: who was there, what you heard, what the light looked like, what you said. Small details are what bring a memory back, and noticing them is a skill that grows the more you write.

example.label: Observation entry
example.text:
The bakery line was out the door at 7 a.m.
An old man in front of me paid for a girl's muffin.
She looked so surprised she forgot to say thanks.
He just winked. I have been smiling about it all day.

sections.h2: Different ways to write it down

blocks.p: A journal entry does not have to be paragraphs. If writing full sentences feels like a chore, change the shape:

ul: **Lists.** Five things that annoyed you, five songs on repeat, five things to do this weekend.
**Bullet notes.** Short fragments, like "slept badly, rainy, good chat with Leo."
**Dialogue.** Write a conversation as a script, including what you wish you had said.
**A letter.** To a friend, a family member, your younger self, or God. You never have to send it.
**A short poem.** It does not need to rhyme. Three lines about the day is enough.
**Doodles and sketches.** Draw your mood as weather, or sketch the view from where you sit.
**A to do list for tomorrow.** Ending the day by writing tomorrow's tasks helps many people sleep.

example.label: Bullet entry
example.text:
Slept badly. Rain all day.
Good chat with Leo about his new job.
Win: finished the tax forms.
Tomorrow: dentist 9:30, return library books, call Gran.

ul: **Spelling and grammar.** Your journal is not homework. Write the way you talk.
**Being interesting.** Ordinary days are worth recording. They are the ones you forget first.
**Writing every day.** Skipping is normal. Just come back.
**Being positive.** Hard feelings belong in a journal too. That is often where it helps most.
**Someone reading it.** Keep it somewhere private. Our [private diary with lock](/private-diary-with-lock/) has a PIN for shared computers.

steps.name: Start with the date and the weather
steps.text: It sounds silly, but writing anything gets your hand moving and the rest often follows.

steps.name: Write "Right now I feel"
steps.text: Finish the sentence. Then write "because" and keep going.

steps.name: Make a list
steps.text: Lists feel easier than paragraphs. Five things that annoyed you, five things you want, five people you love.

steps.name: Set a five minute timer
steps.text: Write without stopping until it rings. If you have nothing to say, write "I have nothing to say" until something comes.

steps.name: Use a prompt
steps.text: Pick one from this page or from [journaling prompts for beginners](/journaling-prompts-for-beginners/) and answer it in a few lines.

blocks.p: If you want a full plan for building the habit, read [how to start a journal](/how-to-start-a-journal/) and [how to journal](/how-to-journal/).

faq.q: What do you write in a journal for beginners?
faq.a: Start with your day in three sentences: what happened, how you felt, and what you think about it. You can also list three things you are grateful for or answer one simple prompt. Keep entries short at first so the habit is easy to keep. Length can grow later once writing feels natural.

faq.q: What should I write in my journal every day?
faq.a: Try a short routine: the date, your mood from 1 to 10, one thing that happened, one thing you are grateful for, and one goal for tomorrow. That takes about five minutes. On days you have more to say, keep writing. On busy days, one line is enough.

faq.q: Is it okay to write negative things in a journal?
faq.a: Yes. A journal is a safe place for anger, sadness and worry. Writing hard feelings down can make them feel smaller and clearer. If you notice you only write when upset, add one good thing at the end of each entry so you see the full picture of your life.

faq.q: How long should a journal entry be?
faq.a: There is no right length. One line counts. Many people write 100 to 300 words, which takes five to ten minutes. Short entries you actually write beat long entries you keep putting off.

faq.q: What do you write on the first page of a journal?
faq.a: Many people write their name, the date they started, and a short note about why they are starting. You could also write a letter to your future self or list what is happening in your life right now. Our guide on [how to start a journal](/how-to-start-a-journal/) has first page ideas.

faq.q: What do you write in a journal when nothing happened?
faq.a: Write what you did anyway, even if it was the same as yesterday. You can also describe one small detail you noticed, how you feel right now, a list of what is on your mind, or answer one prompt. Quiet days are worth recording. They show what normal life looked like, which is often what people most want to remember later.
